newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-Woolworth to close 5-and-10 stores, ending an era.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Woolworth to close 5-and-10 stores, ending an era.

text.p: Woolworth Corp. said Thursday it will close its 400 "five-and-dime" stores where Americans have shopped for baking tins, penny candy and Christmas knick-knacks for 118 years.
The move by the retailer, whose headquarters in lower Manhattan was once the tallest building in the world, was greeted with cheers on Wall Street but tears on Main Street.

"It's so sad," said an employee who gave her name only as Dorine from behind a food counter at a store in Chicago. "I just left a store they closed two years ago. It's almost like a family," said the 20-year veteran, fighting back tears.
The stores being closed have been losing money for years, and so the retailer is pinning its future on stores selling sneakers, sporting goods and other specialty merchandise.

"This is a format that was in vogue in the '20s," Otto Grote, a retail industry analyst at Derby Securities, said of the five-and-dime stores. "A retail concept that is one generation old is one you have to follow closely, but one that is five generations old can be trouble."

Woolworth's stores lost out to new competitors whose stores were larger, such as Wal-Mart Stores Inc., Kmart Corp. and Target, a division of Dayton Hudson Corp. Woolworth, which also said it was changing its name, said the F.W. Woolworth stores were not likely to become profitable anytime soon.
About 9,200 employees will be affected by the store closings. Woolworth said it would transfer some employees and offer severance and outplacement help to others.

Investors cheered the news that Woolworth was exiting a money-losing business. Woolworth stock jumped $2.50 to $27.56 on the New York Stock Exchange. Woolworth said the restructuring would help its results over the next two years.

The decision ends a long attempt to squeeze profits from the stores, which accounted for about $1 billion of the New York-based retailer's annual sales of more than $8 billion. It also ends an era that started in 1879, when the company was founded by Frank W. Woolworth.

"Despite our best efforts and the hard work of the F.W. Woolworth team, the business continued to lose money and it became clear that F.W. Woolworth would be unable, in the foreseeable future, to return to profitability," Chairman Roger Farah said, calling the move a "difficult decision."

The retailer said it will take a charge of about $223 million to convert about 100 of the stores in prime locations to Foot Locker shoe stores, Champs Sports stores or its other specialty formats. It will close or sell the remaining stores and a distribution center in Denver, Pa.
Woolworth's said the closings will take several months.
Employees were told by managers not to comment. "You know, to try to keep morale up," an engineer named Joe said at the Chicago store.
"This is one of the larger stores, and we've been told the smaller stores might close first and they'd ship the merchandise here," he said. "We might be here a year from now, who knows?"
Customers were also saddened by the news.
"I heard it on the news this morning," said a woman leaving the store with a bag of sundries. "They must have a good reason for closing, but it's going to be an inconvenience to a lot of people."
Woolworth said the corporate name change would be made later this year to better reflect its specialty store chains, which also include the Northern Group of clothing stores.

The F.W. Woolworth division lost $24 million on $224 million in sales in the first quarter ended April 26. In 1996, the division generated sales of about $1 billion and an operating loss before one-time items of $37 million.
The unit has stores in 35 states, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands, and has about 3,600 full-time and 5,600 part-time employees.

Woolworth operates 7,558 stores in North America, Europe, Australia and Asia, including Foot Locker, Northern Reflections, After Thoughts and Champs Sports. The company also operates general merchandise stores in Germany, Mexico and Canada.
